subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: On Our Way Back Home — Discussion on how the post office helps people stay connected (p. 19)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 19 — illustration of Navya and her grandfather passing neighbourhood services

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to close their eyes and imagine walking home from school. What do they notice along the way — a shop, a box on a pole, a building with a queue? Students share aloud, and the teacher lists the services named on the board without comment.

Students open Textbook p. 19 and follow Navya and her grandfather's walk. The teacher reads the passage aloud, pausing at the postbox. The class discusses: what is this red box for? Where does a letter go after it is dropped in? The teacher draws a simple arrow diagram on the board: postbox → postman → post office → sorting → destination.

Pairs discuss the question on Textbook p. 19 — 'How does the post office help people stay connected?' Each pair agrees on two reasons and shares with the class. The teacher records key ideas on the board: safety of messages, reaching faraway people, sending parcels.

The teacher closes with an open question: 'Has anyone in your family ever sent or received a letter or parcel? What was in it?' Students respond briefly. The teacher asks students to talk to a family elder about this before the next time the class meets.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how a local public institution connects community members and describe its basic function.
periods.section_context: Postbox, postman, post office, letter sorting by region, parcel delivery, Navya and grandfather's neighbourhood walk.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone has seen a postman in their neighbourhood recently — this bridges the textbook scenario to lived experience. If students mention courier services or WhatsApp, hold that comparison for the communication-timeline unit ahead; here, keep focus on the post office as a physical institution.

periods.activity_title: From Drumbeats to Smartphones: The Communication Timeline
periods.textbook_anchor: On Our Way Back Home — Discussion on how letters taking a long time affected communication in the past and how it differs today (p. 21)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 21 — timeline or illustration showing evolution of communication methods

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'THEN' and 'NOW' as two columns on the board. Students call out communication methods they know — the teacher places each in the correct column without judging or correcting yet. Drumbeats, rock carvings, pigeons, and letters are added if not volunteered.

Students open Textbook p. 21 and read the discussion questions together. The class works through the three prompts: how slow letters affected people in the past; how today's communication differs; and how wrong information can spread quickly online. The teacher facilitates discussion, drawing arrows on the THEN/NOW columns to show the journey from slow to instant.

Small groups of three receive one communication method each (drumbeat, pigeon post, telephone, mobile internet) and discuss: what problem did it solve? What problem remained? Groups share back. The teacher links each answer to the timeline on the board.

The teacher poses the closing question from Textbook p. 21: 'How can we ensure the news we share is true?' Students offer one check each — ask a trusted adult, look at a reliable source, wait before sharing. The teacher affirms the idea of responsibility in communication.

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace how a human-made communication system evolved over time and identify trade-offs introduced by each change.
periods.section_context: Drumbeats, rock carvings, messengers, pigeon post, postal service, telephone, radio, television, mobile phones, internet, slow versus instant communication, misinformation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students what their grandparents used to communicate when they were young — this surfaces intergenerational stories naturally. If students mention local practices such as town criers or temple bells, welcome these as part of the same story of community communication.

periods.textbook_anchor: On Our Way Back Home — Write a letter to a friend and post it (p. 18)
materials: plain A4 or letter paper (one sheet per student)
blackboard showing a model letter format
periods.visual_aids: Blackboard diagram of letter parts: sender's address, date, salutation, body, closing, signature

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a model letter on the board labelling each part — sender's address, date, greeting, body, closing, and signature. The class reads it together. The teacher asks: 'What makes a letter different from a text message?'

Students refer to Textbook p. 18 for the activity prompt and then write their own letter to a friend or family member. They choose their own topic — a recent event, something they noticed on the way to school, a question they want to ask. The teacher circulates, helping with address format and salutation without scripting the content.

Students fold and, if envelopes are available, address their letters. The teacher shows where a postage stamp would go and discusses what happens after a letter is posted, revisiting the postbox-to-destination chain built in the unit where the postal system was first discussed.

Two or three volunteers share one sentence from their letter. The teacher closes by noting that writing a letter is a way of thinking carefully about what you want to say — a skill as valuable today as it was before phones existed.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compose a structured personal message using conventional format and communicate ideas in written form.
periods.section_context: Personal letter writing, sender address, date, salutation, body, closing, signature, postage stamp, envelope addressing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Allow students to write in their home language if they are more comfortable — the skill being developed is structured communication, not English specifically. Ask: 'If you could post this letter anywhere in India, where would you send it and why?'

periods.activity_title: Then and Now: How Elders Communicated
periods.textbook_anchor: On Our Way Back Home — Discuss with elders about communication at their age and compare with today using a table (p. 20)
materials: blackboard with a two-column table drawn

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a two-column table on the board with the headings 'Then (Elders' Time)' and 'Now (Our Time)'. Students are told they are going to act as investigators comparing two eras of communication.

Students open Textbook p. 20, read the table prompt, and copy the table into their notebooks. The teacher leads a structured class sharing: students report what they found out from an elder at home or what they know from family conversations. The teacher fills in the board table as examples accumulate — letters, telegram, landline phone, postcard in the 'Then' column; WhatsApp, video call, email, SMS in the 'Now' column.

Students complete their own tables in their notebooks, adding at least two rows from the class discussion and one row from their own family's story. The teacher circulates and prompts students who have not spoken: 'What does your grandmother use to stay in touch with relatives far away?'

The teacher asks: 'Which method do you think was the most personal? Which is the fastest? Can a method be both?' Students share briefly. The teacher notes that each generation uses what is available — and that the need to stay connected has never changed.

periods.implied_lo: Students can collect information from elders and record observed changes in a community practice across generations in a structured format.
periods.section_context: Elder interview on communication methods, comparison table, letters, telegram, postcard, landline telephone, WhatsApp, video call, email, SMS.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to recall specific stories — 'Did your grandparent mention waiting for a letter for weeks?' — to keep the activity concrete rather than abstract. If students share local communication practices such as sending messages through travelling relatives or seasonal messengers, affirm these as historically real and important.

periods.textbook_anchor: Savings for the Future — Discussion on which money-sending method to choose and why (p. 25)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 25 — illustration of bank, ATM, and money-transfer scenarios

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Where do people keep money to make sure it is safe?' Students respond — piggy bank, at home, bank. The teacher lists answers and circles 'bank', asking what students know about how a bank works.

Students open Textbook p. 25 and read about Navya and her grandfather passing the bank and ATM. The class discusses the three write prompts on p. 25 — whether they save pocket money, where they save it, and why saving is important. The teacher records key reasons on the board: safety, future needs, emergencies.

The teacher introduces the discussion prompt from Textbook p. 25: 'If you had to send money to someone, which method would you choose — phone, money order, or another mode? Why?' Students discuss in pairs and then share. The teacher draws a quick comparison: money order (slow, through post office) versus UPI or mobile transfer (instant, through phone) — connecting to what the class explored earlier about the post office.

The teacher closes with: 'Your grandfather remembers standing in a long queue at the bank. What changed, and what stayed the same about using a bank?' Students respond and the teacher affirms both the continuity (saving for safety) and the change (technology making access easier).

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare traditional and contemporary methods of managing and transferring money and explain the purpose of a bank as a local institution.
periods.section_context: Bank, ATM (Automated Teller Machine), money order, UPI, mobile phone transfer, saving pocket money, piggy bank, bank queue, safety of savings.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether anyone has been inside a bank with a family member — their observations will ground the discussion in real experience. If students mention post office savings accounts or chit funds as savings methods used in their family, welcome these as valid and historically significant savings practices.

periods.textbook_anchor: Savings for the Future — Examine an Indian currency note and answer questions about its value, languages, and symbols (p. 26)
materials: one Indian currency note per group of four (any denomination)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 26 — illustration or photograph of an Indian currency note

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a currency note (or shows the textbook illustration) and asks: 'What do you notice first? What do you think each part means?' Students respond freely.

Students open Textbook p. 26 and read the activity prompt. Groups of four examine a real note and work through the three questions: the denomination value, the number of languages printed on the note, and the pictures or symbols present. Each group records its findings in their notebooks in a short table.

Groups share findings. The teacher facilitates a discussion: Why are so many languages on a single note? What do the symbols or images represent? The teacher connects this to India's linguistic diversity and the note as a shared national document every citizen uses.

The teacher asks: 'The note says a promise from the Reserve Bank of India. What does it mean to promise the value of money?' Students reflect briefly. The teacher notes that this connects banking to trust — the same trust that makes saving in a bank safe.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe a physical document closely and record specific details in a structured format, then connect those details to a broader civic idea.
periods.section_context: Indian currency note, denomination value, languages printed on the note, pictures and symbols on the note, Reserve Bank of India promise, linguistic diversity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Allow each group to choose any denomination they have — observations will differ and comparing across groups enriches the discussion. Ask: 'Do any of the pictures on the note show a place or monument you recognise? Where is it?'

periods.activity_title: My Budget Plan: Spending and Saving ₹100
periods.textbook_anchor: Savings for the Future — Plan how to spend and save ₹100 in a month using a budget table (p. 31)
materials: blackboard showing a blank budget table with columns: Item, Amount to Spend, Amount to Save

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a simple budget table on the board and asks: 'If someone gave you ₹100 for the whole month, what would you do with it?' Students name possible expenses — stationery, snacks, a book. The teacher lists these and asks: 'Is there anything left for saving?'

Students refer to Textbook p. 31, read the budget activity prompt, and create their own budget plan in their notebooks. They decide how much to allocate to stationery, snacks, and at least one saving goal, ensuring the total does not exceed ₹100. The teacher circulates, asking students to explain their choices rather than correcting them.

Students pair up and compare their budgets. Each pair identifies one difference in priorities — for example, one saved more and one spent more on snacks. They agree on one common saving goal they both have.

Pairs share their common saving goal. The teacher connects this back to the bank discussion: saving a little regularly, the same principle a bank account relies on. The teacher closes with: 'How does making a plan before spending help?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can allocate a fixed amount across spending and saving categories and justify their choices in terms of need and future benefit.
periods.section_context: Budget plan, ₹100 allocation, stationery, snacks, toys, piggy bank savings, saving goal, spending priorities.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ensure students know there is no single correct budget — the goal is reasoning about choices, not arithmetic accuracy. Ask: 'If an emergency came up — say you needed a pencil box urgently — would your plan change? How?'

periods.activity_title: Public Places: Who Serves the Neighbourhood?
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — List people who work at a hospital or health centre and their roles (p. 23)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 23 — table of hospital workers

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'When you or someone in your family was not well, where did you go? Who helped you there?' Students share. The teacher lists the places named (hospital, health centre, clinic) and the people (doctor, nurse, pharmacist).

Students open Textbook p. 23 and read the activity prompt. The class co-builds the table of hospital workers and their roles on the board — doctor, nurse, receptionist, ambulance driver, sweeper, pharmacist. The teacher asks students to add anyone they personally know who works at a health centre.

The teacher broadens the discussion: 'The neighbourhood has more than one public place. What about the fire station, the police station, the library?' Students name the workers in each. The teacher draws a quick web on the board: public place in the centre, workers and their roles radiating outward for hospital, post office, and bank — connecting to what the class has already explored in those earlier units.

The teacher asks: 'During a big crisis in your neighbourhood, which of these public places would be the most important? Why?' Students discuss briefly. The teacher notes that all are interconnected — health, safety, communication, and money all support each other.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify workers in multiple public institutions, describe their roles, and explain how these institutions collectively support a community.
periods.section_context: Hospital, health centre, doctors, nurses, ambulance drivers, pharmacists, fire station, police station, library, bus station, public places, health camps, community health workers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students to recall anyone in their community who helped during a local health emergency or flood — this surfaces community solidarity naturally. If students mention ASHA workers, anganwadi workers, or municipal sanitation workers, affirm these as essential neighbourhood roles the textbook's table is beginning to capture.

periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Find out how parents and grandparents travelled to school and compare with today (p. 23)
materials: blackboard with a two-column comparison table
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 22 — pictures of transportation infrastructure including metro trains and flyovers

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a two-column table on the board: 'How they travelled (grandparents/parents)' and 'How we travel today'. Students are told they will fill this from family stories and their own experience.

Students open Textbook p. 23 and read the 'Find out' task. They copy the two-column table into their notebooks and record what they know from family conversations — bullock cart, bicycle, walking long distances, local bus without fixed stops — alongside how they travel today. The teacher circulates and prompts students who are unsure to think about what their grandparents have mentioned.

Students look at Textbook p. 22 — the pictures of metro trains and flyovers. The teacher asks: 'How have these structures made travel faster? What had to be cleared or changed to build them?' Students identify trees, open land, and older buildings. The teacher notes the trade-off Dada ji mentions — faster travel but loss of green space.

The class discusses: 'If your grandparent visited your city today, what would surprise them most about how people travel?' Students respond. The teacher closes with the observation that transport changes shape the neighbourhood's look — connecting back to the map work the class will do.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record changes in transportation across generations using a structured comparison format and identify environmental trade-offs of new infrastructure.
periods.section_context: Metro trains, flyovers, bullock cart, bicycle, walking, local bus, loss of trees and wildlife, environmental trade-off, grandparents' travel, today's transport modes.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students what mode of transport they used to reach school this morning — grounding the historical comparison in their own daily reality. If students mention seasonal transport changes (boat in monsoon, cart in winter), these are regionally real and worth affirming as part of India's transport diversity.

periods.activity_title: Cardinal Directions: Reading Navya's Neighbourhood Map
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Look at the picture and write places located in the North, East, West, and South of Navya's home (p. 28)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 28 — Navya's neighbourhood map with cardinal direction indicator

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a large compass rose on the board with N, S, E, W marked. The teacher asks students to point toward what they think is north in the classroom. After a few responses, the teacher explains how north is fixed and conventionally shown at the top of a map.

Students open Textbook p. 28, look at the map of Navya's neighbourhood, and identify the cardinal direction indicator. Working individually, they write the names of the places located in each of the four directions from Navya's home in their notebooks, following the write prompt on p. 28.

The teacher asks three or four students to share their answers for each direction. Discrepancies are resolved together by returning to the map. The teacher then asks the second task on Textbook p. 28 — imagining their own school at the centre and naming buildings or areas in each direction.

The teacher closes with: 'Why do maps always show north at the top? Is that a rule or a choice?' Students respond. The teacher notes it is a convention — a shared agreement that helps everyone read maps the same way.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use cardinal directions to locate and describe the position of places on a map relative to a central reference point.
periods.section_context: Cardinal directions (N, S, E, W), compass rose, Navya's neighbourhood map, places north/south/east/west of Navya's home, school as central reference point, map convention.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students to use the school building's position (sun rises in the east) to estimate actual directions from where they are sitting — this makes cardinal directions physically real before they work on the textbook map. Encourage students who struggle with the map to trace a line from Navya's home to each direction first.

periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Explain directions to a favourite place using landmarks and direction words (p. 29)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'If a new student joined your class and wanted to find the school canteen from this room, how would you tell them?' Two volunteers give directions. The class notices which words they used — left, right, forward, past the gate.

Students open Textbook p. 29 and read the direction-giving task. They write their own direction paragraph in their notebooks — from school to a favourite nearby place — using at least three landmarks and at least two direction words. The teacher circulates and asks students to be specific: 'Which landmark comes first? What do you turn at?'

Students pair up and read their directions to each other without naming the destination. The partner tries to guess the destination from the directions alone. If the partner cannot guess, the writer identifies which instruction was unclear and rewrites it.

The teacher asks two pairs to share — one whose direction was understood immediately and one where the partner got lost. The class identifies what made the difference: specific landmarks beat vague ones; direction words beat only naming distance. The teacher connects this to why maps use symbols and labels.

periods.implied_lo: Students can communicate a spatial route to a partner using direction words and landmarks with enough clarity for the partner to follow.
periods.section_context: Direction words (left, right, forward, backward), landmarks (park, shop, hospital, bus stop), route from school to a favourite nearby place.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which landmark is the most helpful — a tree, a shop name, or a big building? Why?' This surfaces the idea that good landmarks are stable and distinctive. Accept directions in any language — the spatial reasoning is the skill, not the language of expression.

periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Draw a map showing the route from school to the public library or a nearby public place, marking landmarks (p. 30)
materials: plain A4 paper (one sheet per student)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 30 — example or prompt for the map-drawing activity; Textbook p. 28 — Navya's neighbourhood map as a reference

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays Navya's map from Textbook p. 28 on the board and asks: 'What does Navya use to show direction? What symbols does she use for buildings?' Students identify the compass rose and simple building icons. The teacher explains that the class will now make their own map of the school's neighbourhood.

Students refer to Textbook p. 30 for the map-drawing prompt and draw a map of the route from their school to the public library or another nearby public place of their choice. They mark at least four landmarks — park, shop, hospital, bus stop — and add a north indicator. The teacher circulates, prompting students to use simple symbols consistently and to leave space for labels.

Students add a simple key (legend) to their maps, listing the symbols they have used. The teacher checks that each map has a north indicator, at least three labelled landmarks, a clear route, and a key.

Two or three students place their maps on the desk for a quick gallery view. The class identifies what made each map easy to read — clear labels, consistent symbols, and the direction indicator. The teacher notes that every map is a personal view of a shared space.

periods.implied_lo: Students can create a sketch map of a familiar route using symbols, labels, a direction indicator, and a key to represent spatial information.
periods.section_context: Map of school-to-library route, landmarks (park, shop, hospital, bus stop), compass rose or north indicator, symbols, map key, Navya's neighbourhood map as reference.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Some students may not know the route to a library — allow them to map the route to any nearby public place (bus stop, health centre, market). Ask: 'If you gave your map to a stranger, which part do you think they would find hardest to follow?'

periods.activity_title: Redesigning the Neighbourhood: What Would We Add?
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Discuss what new services or facilities your group would add to improve the neighbourhood (p. 31)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with: 'Imagine you and your group are in charge of making this neighbourhood better. What is missing? What needs improvement?' Each group of four takes one minute to list ideas silently in notebooks before sharing.

Groups discuss the prompt from Textbook p. 31 — what new services or facilities they would add or improve, and how these would help everyone. Each group designates a note-taker. The teacher circulates, prompting groups to think beyond the obvious: 'Who in the neighbourhood might need something you have not thought of yet — older people, young children, people with disabilities?'

Groups present their ideas in turn. The teacher records the most-mentioned suggestions on the board and marks which services from the chapter (hospital, library, post office, park) came up. The class votes — without formal process, just a show of hands — on the one improvement they think would help the most people.

The teacher connects the discussion to civic responsibility: 'Who is responsible for making these changes happen? Is it only the government, or can community members do something too?' Students respond. The teacher draws out the idea of collective action — planting trees, keeping public spaces clean, looking out for neighbours.

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the adequacy of public services in a community setting and propose additions or improvements with reasons grounded in community needs.
periods.section_context: Neighbourhood improvement, public services (hospital, library, park, post office, police station), civic responsibility, collective action, community needs including elderly, children, and people with disabilities.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there anyone in your neighbourhood who does not have easy access to the services you take for granted?' This encourages empathy and equity thinking without being prescriptive. If students propose ideas drawn from regional civic traditions — panchayat meetings, mohalla committees, resident welfare associations — affirm these as real forms of community governance.

periods.activity_title: Community Heroes: People Who Kept Us Safe
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — List neighbourhood people who helped the community during COVID-19 and discuss why it is important to thank them (p. 31)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with: 'Think of a time when your neighbourhood needed a lot of help — perhaps during a big rain, a power cut, or an illness that spread widely. Who came to help?' Students share names and roles. The teacher lists roles on the board without naming individuals.

Students open Textbook p. 31 and read the community helpers discussion prompt. As a class, using input from elders at home and their own knowledge, they build a list of people who helped during a community crisis — doctors, nurses, garbage collectors, shopkeepers, teachers, delivery workers, police officers. Each role is listed with what specific action they took.

Students choose one person from the class list — someone they personally know or heard about from a family elder — and write two sentences in their notebooks: what the person did and why that action mattered to the community. The teacher circulates and prompts students to be specific rather than general.

The teacher asks: 'What can we do to show we value the people who keep our neighbourhood running — not just in a crisis, but every day?' Students offer ideas: saying thank you, not making extra work for sanitation workers, following health advice from doctors. The teacher closes on the theme that neighbourhoods work because people in them take responsibility for each other.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify the contributions of specific community roles during a shared difficulty and articulate why those contributions matter to collective wellbeing.
periods.section_context: Community helpers during COVID-19, doctors, nurses, garbage collectors, shopkeepers, teachers, delivery workers, police officers, gratitude, civic responsibility, daily community interdependence.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students to think of someone not usually celebrated — a sanitation worker, a street-food vendor who stayed open for essential workers — and name what they did. This surfaces the dignity of all labour, which the chapter's equity strand calls for. If students mention locally known figures who helped during regional disasters or floods, affirm these with equal weight.

coverage_handoff.section_context: Cardinal directions (N, S, E, W), compass rose, Navya's neighbourhood map, places north/south/east/west of Navya's home, school as central reference point, map convention.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Look at the picture and write places located in the North, East, West, and South of Navya's home (p. 28)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use Navya's neighbourhood map to identify and record places in each cardinal direction, then apply the same skill to their own school's surroundings.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can communicate a spatial route to a partner using direction words and landmarks with enough clarity for the partner to follow.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Direction words (left, right, forward, backward), landmarks (park, shop, hospital, bus stop), route from school to a favourite nearby place.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Explain directions to a favourite place using landmarks and direction words (p. 29)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write direction instructions from school to a favourite place and test them by having a partner guess the destination from the directions alone.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can create a sketch map of a familiar route using symbols, labels, a direction indicator, and a key to represent spatial information.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Map of school-to-library route, landmarks (park, shop, hospital, bus stop), compass rose or north indicator, symbols, map key, Navya's neighbourhood map as reference.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Draw a map showing the route from school to the public library or a nearby public place, marking landmarks (p. 30)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students draw a personal neighbourhood map of the school-to-library route with symbols, at least four labelled landmarks, a direction indicator, and a key.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the adequacy of public services in a community setting and propose additions or improvements with reasons grounded in community needs.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Neighbourhood improvement, public services (hospital, library, park, post office, police station), civic responsibility, collective action, community needs including elderly, children, and people with disabilities.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Discuss what new services or facilities your group would add to improve the neighbourhood (p. 31)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Groups discuss and present one neighbourhood improvement proposal, then the class connects individual ideas to broader civic responsibility.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify the contributions of specific community roles during a shared difficulty and articulate why those contributions matter to collective wellbeing.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Community helpers during COVID-19, doctors, nurses, garbage collectors, shopkeepers, teachers, delivery workers, police officers, gratitude, civic responsibility, daily community interdependence.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — List neighbourhood people who helped the community during COVID-19 and discuss why it is important to thank them (p. 31)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students build a class list of community helpers from a crisis period, write two sentences about one helper's contribution, and discuss everyday civic responsibility.

assessment_items.question_text: A letter is dropped into a postbox near Navya's school. What happens to it next, before it reaches the person it was sent to?

options.label: A
options.text: A postman collects it and delivers it directly to the address on the envelope the same day.

options.label: B
options.text: A postman collects it, it is sorted at the post office by region, and then it is dispatched to its destination.

options.label: C
options.text: The letter is taken to the nearest telephone exchange and scanned before being sent.

options.label: D
options.text: The letter stays in the postbox until the receiver comes to collect it from there.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer describes the full postal chain: collection → sorting by region → dispatch. Accept any response that names all three stages in order.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how a local public institution connects community members and describe its basic function.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student understands that the postman is involved but believes delivery is direct and immediate — missing the sorting step that makes the postal system work across regions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses a postbox with a post office counter and has not grasped that letters are actively collected and processed rather than waiting for the recipient.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has conflated two different communication systems — postal and telephone — suggesting the timeline of communication evolution has not yet been consolidated.

assessment_items.question_text: People have communicated with each other in many ways through history — from drumbeats and rock carvings to mobile phones and the internet. Choose TWO communication methods from different time periods. For each one, write (a) one problem it solved and (b) one limitation it still had.
expected_elements: Names two communication methods from clearly different time periods (e.g. one ancient or pre-modern and one modern).
States a specific problem each method solved — not just 'it was faster' but what difficulty it addressed.
States a specific limitation for each method — slow delivery, lack of reach, cost, risk of misinformation, etc.
Shows awareness that each change brought a new trade-off, not only improvement.
assessment_items.annotation: Award marks for quality of reasoning about the trade-off, not for naming the most recent technology. Pigeon post, postcard, telephone, and mobile internet are all valid choices. A student who names only modern methods has not demonstrated the evolutionary arc.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how a human-made communication system evolved over time and identify trade-offs introduced by each change.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Names two communication methods from clearly different time periods (e.g. one ancient or pre-modern and one modern).
States a specific problem each method solved — not just 'it was faster' but what difficulty it addressed.
States a specific limitation for each method — slow delivery, lack of reach, cost, risk of misinformation, etc.
Shows awareness that each change brought a new trade-off, not only improvement.

assessment_items.task: Write a letter to a relative or friend who lives in another town. Tell them about one interesting thing you have seen or done recently. Use the correct letter format: your address, the date, a greeting, the main message, a closing, and your name.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Your address: ___
Date: ___
Dear ___,
[Write your message here — at least three sentences about something you saw or did.]
Your friend / Your loving ___,
[Your name]
format_of_output: A handwritten letter on the sheet provided, using all six parts of the format.
assessment_items.annotation: Credit the presence of all six format parts and the coherence of the message. The content of the message is the student's choice — do not penalise for topic. Accept letters written in any Indian language.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compose a structured personal message using conventional format and communicate ideas in written form.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply the conventional structure of a personal letter to communicate a real message, showing that written communication follows shared rules that make it readable by others.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold provides the six format slots in order. A strong response fills all six with appropriate content; a weak response omits parts or confuses the order (e.g. puts the date at the end).
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: all six parts present, message is at least three coherent sentences, appropriate greeting and closing. Weak: two or more parts missing, message is a single word or unrelated to the prompt.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Accept letters in any Indian language. Students who cannot yet write a full letter may dictate it to a scribe or draw key scenes with labels — the format structure is still being demonstrated.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The letter format is itself the skill being assessed — the physical act of writing and laying out the parts mirrors the chapter's activity and makes the output collectible as evidence.

assessment_items.question_text: Riya interviewed her grandmother for a class activity. Her grandmother said: 'When I was your age, I used to wait weeks for news from relatives who lived far away.' Which pair of communication methods BEST shows what changed between her grandmother's time and today?

options.label: A
options.text: Handwritten letter sent by post (then) → WhatsApp message (now)

assessment_items.annotation: Option A correctly pairs the slow written-letter era with the instant messaging era, mapping directly onto the grandmother's description of waiting weeks. Options C and D involve technologies that are either both modern or only marginally different in era.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can collect information from elders and record observed changes in a community practice across generations in a structured format.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has not connected the grandmother's story to communication specifically — television and cinema are entertainment, not personal communication methods, indicating a category confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student recognises that both items are communication technologies but has not noticed that mobile phones and the internet are both contemporary — there is no generational contrast.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has chosen two written communication methods from overlapping eras — postcard and telegram are both pre-digital — showing the generational shift has not been grasped.

assessment_items.question_text: Navya's grandfather remembered standing in long queues at the bank and sending money to relatives through money orders at the post office. Today, people use UPI on their phones for instant transfers. (a) Name ONE way banks help people that is NOT about sending money. (b) What is an ATM and how does it help people who need cash urgently?
expected_elements: Names a bank function other than money transfer — e.g. keeping savings safe, giving loans, providing a passbook record, offering a savings account.
Defines ATM as Automated Teller Machine or describes it as a machine that gives cash at any time of day.
Explains one specific benefit of the ATM — available round the clock, no need to wait for a bank to open, accessible cash in emergencies.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for any accurate non-transfer bank function in part (a). For part (b), the definition and the benefit are two separate marks — a student who only defines ATM without explaining the benefit earns partial credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare traditional and contemporary methods of managing and transferring money and explain the purpose of a bank as a local institution.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

expected_elements: Names a bank function other than money transfer — e.g. keeping savings safe, giving loans, providing a passbook record, offering a savings account.
Defines ATM as Automated Teller Machine or describes it as a machine that gives cash at any time of day.
Explains one specific benefit of the ATM — available round the clock, no need to wait for a bank to open, accessible cash in emergencies.

assessment_items.question_text: Arjun examined a ₹50 currency note in class. He noticed writing in many languages and a picture of a famous building. What do the many languages printed on an Indian currency note tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: Each language on the note belongs to a different bank that printed a separate version.

options.label: B
options.text: India has many languages and the note is meant to be used and understood across the whole country.

options.label: C
options.text: People must learn all the languages on the note before they are allowed to use it.

options.label: D
options.text: The note was printed in different countries and each language comes from a different nation.

assessment_items.annotation: Option A connects the observation (many languages) to the civic idea (national unity in diversity). Options B and D reflect misconceptions about how currency is issued; Option C is an implausible but internally coherent misconception about language as a prerequisite for use.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe a physical document closely and record specific details in a structured format, then connect those details to a broader civic idea.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has not connected the currency note to a single national institution — the Reserve Bank of India — and instead imagines multiple national origins, suggesting the civic function of currency has not been grasped.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student treats the languages as a user requirement rather than an inclusive design feature, showing a misreading of the observation step.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has confused the idea of multiple languages with multiple issuing authorities, suggesting the concept of a single central bank is not yet secure.

assessment_items.task: You have ₹100 to use over a whole month. Create your budget plan. Decide how much you will spend on different things and how much you will save. Then write one sentence explaining why you chose to save the amount you did.
assessment_items.scaffold:
| What I will spend on | Amount (₹) |
|---|---|
| ___ | ___|
| ___ | ___|
| ___ | ___|
| **Total spending** | ___|
| **Amount I will save** | ___|

Why I chose this saving amount: ___
format_of_output: A completed budget table with at least two spending categories, a saving amount, and a total that does not exceed ₹100.
One written sentence justifying the saving choice.
assessment_items.annotation: The total of spending plus saving must equal ₹100 or less — accept any allocation as long as arithmetic is consistent and the justification sentence refers to a future need or benefit. There is no single correct budget.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can allocate a fixed amount across spending and saving categories and justify their choices in terms of need and future benefit.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply the concept of saving to a personal financial decision, making explicit the reasoning that connects present restraint to future benefit.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The table has space for at least two spending categories and a saving row. A strong response fills all rows with plausible amounts and a coherent justification. A weak response leaves the saving row blank or gives a justification that does not refer to future benefit.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: at least two spending categories, saving amount greater than zero, total ≤ ₹100, justification names a specific future goal or emergency. Weak: saving amount is zero with no reason, or total exceeds ₹100 showing the constraint was not applied.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who are unfamiliar with pocket money may use school supplies or household items as spending categories — the skill is proportional allocation, not familiarity with consumer spending.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The table format mirrors the textbook activity and makes the allocation explicit and checkable, while the written sentence requires the student to articulate the purpose of saving rather than just perform the arithmetic.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the list of public places in a neighbourhood: hospital, library, post office, police station, fire station, bus station. Choose TWO of these places. For each one, name ONE type of worker who works there and describe ONE thing that worker does to help the community.
expected_elements: Names two different public places from the list provided.
Names a worker who genuinely works in each chosen place (e.g. nurse at hospital, librarian at library, postman at post office).
Describes a specific action or role for each worker — not just a job title — that explains how the community benefits.
Shows understanding that these institutions serve the community collectively, not just individual users.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any worker plausibly associated with the chosen institution. Credit the specificity of the described action — 'gives medicine' is stronger than 'helps people'. Regional-variation note: workers named may include ASHA workers, anganwadi workers, or municipal staff — these are all valid and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify workers in multiple public institutions, describe their roles, and explain how these institutions collectively support a community.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

expected_elements: Names two different public places from the list provided.
Names a worker who genuinely works in each chosen place (e.g. nurse at hospital, librarian at library, postman at post office).
Describes a specific action or role for each worker — not just a job title — that explains how the community benefits.
Shows understanding that these institutions serve the community collectively, not just individual users.

assessment_items.question_text: Meera's grandfather walked to school every day through fields and forests. Today, Meera takes the metro to school. (a) Give ONE way this change in transport has made daily life easier. (b) Give ONE thing that was lost or harmed when the metro line was built through the neighbourhood.
expected_elements: Names a specific benefit of the metro — faster travel, reaching more places, less time spent commuting.
Names a specific loss associated with building the metro — trees cut down, birds and animals displaced, open land built over.
Demonstrates understanding that new infrastructure involves a trade-off, not only improvement.
assessment_items.annotation: Award marks for both the benefit and the specific loss. A response that gives only a benefit or only a loss is incomplete. Accept any plausible environmental or social loss connected to infrastructure construction.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record changes in transportation across generations using a structured comparison format and identify environmental trade-offs of new infrastructure.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

expected_elements: Names a specific benefit of the metro — faster travel, reaching more places, less time spent commuting.
Names a specific loss associated with building the metro — trees cut down, birds and animals displaced, open land built over.
Demonstrates understanding that new infrastructure involves a trade-off, not only improvement.

assessment_items.question_text: Navya's map shows her home at the centre. The library is to the north of her home, the park is to the east, the hospital is to the south, and the post office is to the west. Navya walks out of her home toward the post office. In which direction is she walking?
assessment_items.annotation: The answer is West, directly stated in the question's map description. This tests whether the student can read a directional description and identify the corresponding cardinal direction without a visual map.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use cardinal directions to locate and describe the position of places on a map relative to a central reference point.

competency.competency_text: Draws a sketch of their school, village, and ward using symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has reversed east and west — a common confusion when working from verbal description rather than a physical map. May need additional practice orienting with a compass rose.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have associated the first direction mentioned (north — library) with the direction of movement, suggesting the map description was not read systematically.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have confused the hospital (south) with the destination, suggesting they recall a direction from the list but do not match it to the specific place asked about.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya wants to give her friend directions from school to the nearest hospital. Write THREE clear direction instructions she should give, using direction words (left, right, forward, backward) and at least TWO landmarks.
expected_elements: Gives exactly three direction instructions in a logical sequence (each building on the last).
Uses at least two direction words from the set: left, right, forward, backward.
Names at least two landmarks — these may be a park, shop, bus stop, or any identifiable feature near the student's school.
The instructions form a coherent route — a reader following them would reach a destination rather than going in circles.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional-variation note: the specific landmarks named will differ by school location and are all correct — credit any landmark the student considers identifiable near their school. The hospital in the question is illustrative; accept directions to any nearby public place if the student notes their school has no hospital nearby.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can communicate a spatial route to a partner using direction words and landmarks with enough clarity for the partner to follow.

competency.competency_text: Draws a sketch of their school, village, and ward using symbols and directions

expected_elements: Gives exactly three direction instructions in a logical sequence (each building on the last).
Uses at least two direction words from the set: left, right, forward, backward.
Names at least two landmarks — these may be a park, shop, bus stop, or any identifiable feature near the student's school.
The instructions form a coherent route — a reader following them would reach a destination rather than going in circles.

assessment_items.task: Draw a map of the route from your school to any nearby public place (library, bus stop, park, or hospital). On your map, mark at least FOUR landmarks, add a north indicator (compass rose or arrow), and draw a key (legend) that explains the symbols you used.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Steps to follow:
1. Draw your school at the centre or one edge of the page.
2. Draw the route as a path or road.
3. Mark at least four landmarks along the route using simple symbols.
4. Add a north indicator — an arrow or compass rose — at the top of the map.
5. Draw a small key at the corner showing what each symbol means.
format_of_output: A hand-drawn map on the sheet provided.
A key listing at least three symbols used.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional-variation note: landmarks and the destination will differ by location — all are correct. Credit the presence and legibility of the required map elements (route, four landmarks, north indicator, key) rather than artistic quality. A map in any script is acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can create a sketch map of a familiar route using symbols, labels, a direction indicator, and a key to represent spatial information.

competency.competency_text: Draws a sketch of their school, village, and ward using symbols and directions

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate spatial knowledge of a familiar environment into a symbolic representation using the conventions of map-making — direction, symbols, labels, and a key.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The five-step scaffold leads the student through the map in construction order. A strong response follows the sequence and produces all five elements. A weak response omits the key or north indicator, suggesting the student drew a picture rather than a map.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: route is clear, four or more landmarks are labelled and symbolised, north indicator is present, key has at least three symbols. Weak: landmarks are unlabelled, no north indicator, no key, or the map has no identifiable route.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot draw clearly may label with words instead of symbols — the spatial reasoning is the skill. Students unfamiliar with the area around school may map the route from home to school instead.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The map format directly mirrors the chapter's map-drawing activity and produces a concrete, collectable artefact the teacher can assess against specific map-elements criteria.

assessment_items.question_text: Your neighbourhood currently has a post office, a bank, and a small clinic. A group of residents wants to add two new public services. Choose TWO services you would recommend adding. For each one, explain who would benefit and why that service is needed in the neighbourhood.
look_for: Names two public services not already listed in the question (e.g. library, police station, fire station, park, community centre).
Identifies a specific group of community members who would benefit from each service — elderly residents, young children, people who are unwell, those without private transport.
Explains a concrete need the service meets — not just 'it would be nice' but a specific gap in the neighbourhood's current provision.
Shows awareness that public services are for everyone, not only for those with money or status.
Optional but strong: connects the two chosen services to show how they complement each other in supporting the community.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional-variation note: the specific services recommended will reflect students' local contexts — urban, rural, and semi-urban neighbourhoods will have different gaps. All contextually reasoned responses are valid. Credit the quality of reasoning about community need, not the particular services chosen.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the adequacy of public services in a community setting and propose additions or improvements with reasons grounded in community needs.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

look_for: Names two public services not already listed in the question (e.g. library, police station, fire station, park, community centre).
Identifies a specific group of community members who would benefit from each service — elderly residents, young children, people who are unwell, those without private transport.
Explains a concrete need the service meets — not just 'it would be nice' but a specific gap in the neighbourhood's current provision.
Shows awareness that public services are for everyone, not only for those with money or status.
Optional but strong: connects the two chosen services to show how they complement each other in supporting the community.

assessment_items.task: Think of ONE person in your neighbourhood (or a person you have heard about from a family elder) who helped the community during a difficult time — like a health crisis, a flood, or a power cut. Write their role, what they did, and ONE sentence explaining why their help mattered to the people around them.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Person's role (e.g. nurse, shopkeeper, teacher): ___
What they did: ___
Why their help mattered: ___
format_of_output: Three completed lines using the scaffold — role, action, and explanation of why it mattered.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional-variation note: the person named and the crisis described will vary by student and region — all are valid. Credit the specificity of the action described and the coherence of the explanation of why it mattered. A student who names a well-known public figure rather than a local person should still receive credit if they describe a specific action.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the contributions of specific community roles during a shared difficulty and articulate why those contributions matter to collective wellbeing.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can draw on community knowledge — from personal experience or elder testimony — to name a specific contribution and explain its significance to others, demonstrating civic awareness and the ability to value diverse forms of community service.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three-line scaffold separates role, action, and significance. A strong response fills all three with specific, distinct content. A weak response repeats the same idea across all three lines or leaves the 'why it mattered' line as 'it was helpful'.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a specific role, a concrete action (not just 'helped'), and an explanation that names who benefited and how. Weak: vague role (e.g. 'a good person'), no specific action, and a justification that is circular ('it mattered because it was important').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot think of a real person may describe a role type (sanitation worker, neighbourhood shopkeeper) and invent a plausible action — the reflective skill is still demonstrated. Accept responses in any language.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The scaffold enforces the three-part structure (role → action → significance) that the implied learning outcome requires — it prevents students from writing only a name and stopping, and makes the quality of reasoning visible to the teacher.
